segments.text: A radar has a problem that no other sensor has.
To find an aircraft, it has to shout, and almost anything can hear a shout.
A simple receiver on the aircraft picks up the radar's pulse on its way out, while the
radar has to wait for a tiny fraction of the same pulse to bounce back.
The radar's signal has to make the whole trip twice, so a pilot can know they are being
watched well before the radar can see them, and the radar is the only one in the conversation
announcing its position to the whole sky.
So, here is the question, how does a machine that is so exposed manage to be the foundation
of every air defense, every warship, and every air traffic system on Earth?
The answer is a chain of compromises, because the physics of an echo is brutal.
Each design choice in a radar is a decision about which part of that brutality to put up
with.
Start with the principle, which is simple enough to explain in a sentence.
A radar sends out a short burst of radio waves, which travel at the speed of light, and listens
for the echo.
The time between the burst and the echo gives the distance.
A delay of one millionth of a second means a target about 150 meters away, so a delay
of a thousandth means a target 150 kilometers off.
The dish turns, and the direction it was pointing when the echo came back gives the bearing.
Everything else in radar is an effort to make those two measurements sharper.
Then comes the harsh part.
The echo is unbelievably weak.
The energy that leaves the antenna spreads out in a widening sphere, and the small portion
that hits the aircraft spreads out again as it returns.
The result is that the power coming back falls with the fourth power of the distance.
Double the range and the echo is 16 times fainter.
To see twice as far, a radar must be 16 times more powerful, or far more sensitive.
That one fact explains why long-range radars are enormous, and why a small increase in range
is so expensive.
There is also a timing problem.
A radar must wait for the echo of one pulse before it can safely send the next, and the
pause between pulses sets how far it can see without confusion.
Send pulses quickly and the radar can measure speed well, but an echo from a far target may
arrive after the next pulse and be read as a near one.
Send them slowly and range is clear, but speed becomes blurred.
Radars therefore alternate between modes, using different rhythms for different jobs, and
no single rhythm is right for everything.
There are only so many ways to deal with an echo that faint.
One is to send more power, which is why large radars use megawatts.
Another is a bigger antenna, which collects more of what returns and focuses the beam more
narrowly.
And that is why the biggest warning radars look like the sides of buildings.
A third is to listen for longer, adding up many echoes from many pulses until the target
rises out of the noise.
All of them cost something.
More power makes the radar easier to find.
A bigger antenna is harder to move, and listening longer is slower.
Which wavelength to use is the next decision, and it shows how a radar is built for a purpose.
Long waves, in the very high frequency band, bend around the curve of the earth a little,
and pass through weather easily, and a radar that uses them can see far.
But they cannot tell two close targets apart, and the position they give is rough.
Short waves, in the bands used by fire control radars, give a tight beam and fine detail,
but they are absorbed by rain, and cannot reach as far.
The radar that finds a target, and the radar that guides a missile onto it, are rarely the same set.
A second thing that radar measures is movement, and it does this using the Doppler effect.
An echo from something coming closer comes back at a slightly higher frequency, and from something moving
away it comes back lower, in the same way that a siren's pitch changes as it passes.
This is how a radar separates an aircraft from a hillside.
The hill returns an echo that does not shift, and the aircraft returns one that does.
It is a filter that throws away everything standing still.
It also has a weakness, because an aircraft flying exactly across the radar's line of sight
creates almost no shift, and can disappear into the clutter.
A target's size, as the radar sees it, is also not what it looks like to the eye.
What counts is how much energy comes back, called the radar cross-section,
and it depends on shape and material as much as on bulk.
A flat metal plate turned square to the beam is a brilliant mirror,
while the same plate tilted a few degrees sends the beam off into the sky.
A large aircraft shaped to turn the beam aside can return less than a small bird,
and a corner can return more than a sphere ten times its size.
The radar measures the echo, and the echo is a property of geometry.
That is worth stopping on, because clutter is the real enemy of radar, more than the distance.
The ground, the sea, rain, and flocks of birds all send echoes, and a target must be picked out from
among them. A radar looking down at a low-flying aircraft is looking at a patch of ground that is
much brighter than the thing flying over it. Much of the engineering inside a radar is not about
seeing, it is about deciding what not to see. Radar also cannot see around the world. Radio waves
travel in straight lines, and the earth curves away, so there is a horizon beyond which nothing is visible,
and a low-flying aircraft can stay under it until it is close. A radar mounted high on a mast sees
further, and one carried on an aircraft sees much further. This is the reason a country with a coast
and a lot of sea builds a chain of stations or flies radar aircraft, and why a hill in the wrong place
can matter more than the electronics on top of it. The history shows how radical this was. In 1940,
Britain strung a line of tall towers along its southern and eastern coasts, which sent out signals and
received echoes from aircraft crossing the channel. The system was crude. It could not see low, and
its answers were relayed by telephone to a room where operators moved markers on a table. But it told
the fighter squadrons when the raiders were coming and roughly where, so they did not have to be in
the air all day. Radar did not win the Battle of Britain alone, but it allowed a smaller air force to
be in the right place. The old radars had a physical dish that turned, and the new ones have none.
A modern phased array radar is a flat panel made of thousands of small transmitters and receivers,
and by shifting the timing of each one, it steers the beam without moving anything. It can point in
a new direction in microseconds, track dozens of targets at once, and keep searching in between.
The panel can lose several modules and still work, and a warship can carry four flat panels on its
superstructure and watch every direction at once without turning a single part. Some of these can also
switch between searching, tracking, and even guiding missiles in the same second. There is a cost,
and it is money, because each module is a small, precise radio of its own.
What does the radar's enemy do about it? The answer is that a radar can be jammed by a transmitter that
pours noise into its receiver, or deceived by something that sends back a false echo. It can be
avoided by flying low or by hugging terrain, and it can be hunted. Special missiles home onto the radar's
own signal, and fly down the beam to the antenna. So the radar that stays on becomes a target,
and a good operator switches off, moves, and switches back on somewhere else. A radar crew's
survival depends on being silent. Which brings us to what is easy to get wrong. People talk about
radar as if it either sees an aircraft or does not. In truth, it works in probabilities. At each distance,
there is a chance of detecting a given target, and the chance falls as the distance grows and the
target gets smaller, and the clutter gets worse. A radar that is said to see a hundred kumliters is
really a radar that sees a certain type of target at that range, with a certain probability. That is
my own way of putting it, but it suggests that a radar has no range, it has a curve. So return to
the radar that has to shout, and the aircraft that hears it first. Every part of the set, the powerful
pulse, the huge antenna, the filter that discards what stands still, the chain of towers, and the tiles of
the phased array, exists to get more information out of an echo that is almost not there. A radar
does not see the sky. It reconstructs it from a whisper in a room that is becoming louder every year.
